Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Renewable energy sources play an increasingly important role in the global energy mix, as the effort to reduce the environmental impact of energy production increases.

Out of all the renewable energy alternatives, wind energy is one of the most developed technologies worldwide. The U.S Department of Energy has put together a guide to achieving operational efficiency using predictive maintenance practices.

Predictive maintenance uses sensor information and analysis methods to measure and predict degradation and future component capability. The idea behind predictive maintenance is that failure patterns are predictable and if component failure can be predicted accurately and the component is replaced before it fails, the costs of operation and maintenance will be much lower.

The sensors fitted across different machines involved in the process of energy generation collect data related to various environmental factors (temperature, humidity, wind speed, etc.) and additional features related to various parts of the wind turbine (gearbox, tower, blades, break, etc.).

Objective¶

“ReneWind” is a company working on improving the machinery/processes involved in the production of wind energy using machine learning and has collected data of generator failure of wind turbines using sensors. They have shared a ciphered version of the data, as the data collected through sensors is confidential (the type of data collected varies with companies). Data has 40 predictors, 20000 observations in the training set and 5000 in the test set.

The objective is to build various classification models, tune them, and find the best one that will help identify failures so that the generators could be repaired before failing/breaking to reduce the overall maintenance cost. The nature of predictions made by the classification model will translate as follows:

  • True positives (TP) are failures correctly predicted by the model. These will result in repairing costs.
  • False negatives (FN) are real failures where there is no detection by the model. These will result in replacement costs.
  • False positives (FP) are detections where there is no failure. These will result in inspection costs.

It is given that the cost of repairing a generator is much less than the cost of replacing it, and the cost of inspection is less than the cost of repair.

“1” in the target variables should be considered as “failure” and “0” represents “No failure”.

Data Description¶

The data provided is a transformed version of the original data which was collected using sensors.

  • Train.csv - To be used for training and tuning of models.
  • Test.csv - To be used only for testing the performance of the final best model.

Both the datasets consist of 40 predictor variables and 1 target variable.

Data Overview¶

  • Train shape: 20,000 × 41
  • Test shape: 5,000 × 40
  • Predictors: All numeric (ciphered sensor values)
  • Target variable: Binary (1 = failure, 0 = no failure)
  • Class distribution: 94.45% no failure, 5.55% failure → highly imbalanced
  • Missing values: 18 in V1 and V2 (<0.1%), others complete
  • Duplicates: None

Univariate Analysis Observations¶

  • Most features follow an approximately symmetric bell-shaped distribution (close to normal).
  • A few variables show slight skewness (e.g., V1, V8, V32... etc).
  • Some variables have longer tails/outliers on either side (e.g., V4, V21, V27.. etc).
  • Feature ranges differ slightly (some spread between -15 to 15, others narrower like -5 to 5).
  • Overall distributions look stable as no extreme anomalies are spotted.

Data Preprocessing¶

In [16]:
# From earlier analysis we know that 2 columns have 18 missing values, Let's fix them using median imputation

from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
train_imputed = train.copy()
train_imputed.iloc[:, :-1] = imputer.fit_transform(train.iloc[:, :-1])

# As features are continuous with varying ranges, we will use StandardScaler for scaling
# This will ensure each feature has mean 0 and standard deviation 1

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X = train_imputed.drop(columns=["Target"])
y = train_imputed["Target"]

X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
In [19]:
# Now, lets split the data into training and validation sets - We will use test.csv only for final evaluation

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2,  stratify=y)

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Error Cost Trade-off¶

  • False Negatives (FN): The most costly error, since missing a failure leads to full generator replacement.
  • False Positives (FP): Lower cost, only leads to additional inspection.
  • True Positives (TP): Lead to repairs, which are cheaper than replacements.

Hence, we will priortize Recall as the main evaluation criterion, while using F1 as a secondary evaluation metrics.

Initial Model Building (Model 0)¶

  • Let's start with a neural network consisting of
    • just one hidden layer
    • activation function of ReLU
    • SGD as the optimizer
In [20]:
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense
from tensorflow.keras.optimizers import SGD
In [21]:
model = Sequential([
    Dense(32, activation='relu', input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)),  
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')  
])

C:\Users\eriander\AppData\Roaming\Python\Python312\site-packages\keras\src\layers\core\dense.py:92: UserWarning: Do not pass an `input_shape`/`input_dim` argument to a layer. When using Sequential models, prefer using an `Input(shape)` object as the first layer in the model instead.
  super().__init__(activity_regularizer=activity_regularizer, **kwargs)
In [22]:
optimizer = SGD(learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9)
model.compile(optimizer=optimizer, 
              loss='binary_crossentropy', 
              metrics=['accuracy', 
                       tf.keras.metrics.Recall(name='recall'),
                       tf.keras.metrics.F1Score(name='f1_score', average='micro', threshold=0.5)])
In [23]:
history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, 
                    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
                    epochs=20, batch_size=32, verbose=1)

Model 1: Neural Network (ReLU, SGD, class weights)¶

  • Accuracy: ~98% (train & val)
  • Recall: ~0.88–0.92 → most positives detected
  • F1-score: rose to ~0.83 (val)
  • Loss: smooth decline, no major overfitting

Insight: Class weights boosted recall (fewer false negatives) while maintaining strong F1 and overall stability.

Model 2¶

In [29]:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Input
In [30]:
model2 = Sequential([
    Input(shape=(X_train.shape[1],)),       # input layer
    Dense(128, activation='relu'),          # hidden layer 1
    Dense(64, activation='relu'),           # hidden layer 2
    Dense(32, activation='relu'),           # hidden layer 3
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')          # output layer
])
In [31]:
model2.compile(
    optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9),
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=[
        'accuracy',
        recall,
        f1_score
    ]
)
In [32]:
history2 = model2.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=64,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    class_weight=class_weights,
    verbose=1
)

Model 2: Deeper Neural Network (ReLU, SGD, class weights)¶

  • Accuracy: ~98–99% (train & val)
  • Recall: ~0.87–0.94 (strong positive detection)
  • F1-score: peaked ~0.88 (val)
  • Loss: steadily decreased, occasional fluctuations but no major overfitting

Model 3¶

In [33]:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dropout
In [34]:
model3 = Sequential([
    Dense(128, activation="relu", input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)),
    Dropout(0.2),
    Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    Dropout(0.1),
    Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")
])
In [35]:
from tensorflow.keras.optimizers import Adam
In [36]:
model3.compile(
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
    loss="binary_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy", f1_score, recall]
)
In [37]:
history3 = model3.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=128,
    class_weight=class_weights,
    verbose=1
)

Model 3: Neural Network with Adam Optimizer (Class Weights and DropOuts Applied)¶

Performance Summary¶

  • Training Accuracy: ~98%
  • Validation Accuracy: ~98–99%
  • Training F1-score: ~0.83–0.85
  • Validation F1-score: ~0.87–0.89
  • Training Recall: ~0.92
  • Validation Recall: ~0.89–0.90
  • Final Loss: Training ~0.13, Validation ~0.09

Model 4¶

In [38]:
model4 = Sequential([
    Dense(128, activation='relu', input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)),
    Dropout(0.3),

    Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.2),

    Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.1),

    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])
In [39]:
model4.compile(
    optimizer= Adam(),
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy', f1_score, recall]
)
In [40]:
history4 = model4.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=64,
    class_weight=class_weights,
    verbose=1
)

Model 4: Deeper Neural Network with Dropout & Adam¶

  • Train Accuracy: ~98.5%
  • Validation Accuracy: ~99.0%
  • Train F1-score: ~0.87
  • Validation F1-score: ~0.91–0.92
  • Validation Recall: ~0.89–0.91

Model 5¶

In [41]:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import BatchNormalization
In [42]:
model5 = Sequential([
    Dense(128, activation='relu', input_dim=X_train.shape[1]),
    BatchNormalization(),
    Dropout(0.3),
    
    Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    BatchNormalization(),
    Dropout(0.2),
    
    Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    BatchNormalization(),
    Dropout(0.1),
    
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])
In [43]:
model5.compile(
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy', f1_score, recall]
)
In [44]:
history5 = model5.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=64,
    class_weight=class_weights,
    verbose=1
)

Model 6¶

from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping, ReduceLROnPlateau
In [46]:
model6 = Sequential([
    Dense(128, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.3),

    Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.2),

    Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.1),

    Dense(16, activation='relu'),

    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])
In [47]:
model6.compile(
    optimizer=Adam(),
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy', f1_score, recall]
)
In [48]:
early_stop = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)
reduce_lr = ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor='val_loss', factor=0.5, patience=3, verbose=1)

history6 = model6.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    epochs=40,
    batch_size=64,
    class_weight=class_weights,
    callbacks=[early_stop, reduce_lr],
    verbose=1
)

Model 6: Adam + Dropouts + Early Stopping for training¶

Validation Performance:

  • Accuracy: ~99.1%
  • F1 Score: ~0.92
  • Recall: ~0.90
  • Loss: ~0.09–0.12

Model Performance Comparison and Final Model Selection¶

Now, in order to select the final model, we will compare the performances of all the models for the training and validation sets.

In [49]:
models = [model, model1, model2, model3, model4, model5, model6]
histories = [history, history2, history3, history4, history5, history6]
In [50]:
best_f1_metrics = []

for i, h in enumerate(histories):
    val_f1 = h.history['val_f1_score']
    best_epoch = val_f1.index(max(val_f1))  # epoch with highest F1
    best_val_f1 = val_f1[best_epoch]
    best_val_recall = h.history['val_recall'][best_epoch]

    best_f1_metrics.append((i, best_val_f1, best_val_recall))

# Print all models' best validation F1
for idx, f1, recall in best_f1_metrics:
    print(f"Model {idx}: Best Val F1 = {f1:.4f}, Best Val Recall = {recall:.4f}")

Model 0: Best Val F1 = 0.8821, Best Val Recall = 0.9099
Model 1: Best Val F1 = 0.9108, Best Val Recall = 0.8739
Model 2: Best Val F1 = 0.9009, Best Val Recall = 0.9009
Model 3: Best Val F1 = 0.9327, Best Val Recall = 0.9054
Model 4: Best Val F1 = 0.9241, Best Val Recall = 0.9054
Model 5: Best Val F1 = 0.9346, Best Val Recall = 0.9009

Now, let's check the performance of the final model on the test set.

In [51]:
# First applying all the scaling and imputation steps to the test data
X_test = test.copy()
X_test.iloc[:, :-1] = imputer.transform(X_test.iloc[:, :-1])
X_test = scaler.transform(X_test.drop(columns=["Target"]))
y_test = test["Target"]
In [52]:
final_model = model6 # Choosing model 6 because it had a better balance of recall and F1
test_loss, test_accuracy, test_f1, test_recall = final_model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=1)

print(f"Test Loss: {test_loss:.4f}")
print(f"Test Accuracy: {test_accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"Test F1 Score: {test_f1:.4f}")
print(f"Test Recall: {test_recall:.4f}")

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Business Impact Analysis¶

Model Performance Summary¶

The final neural network model (Model 6) achieved excellent performance on the test set:

  • Test Accuracy: 98.86%
  • Test F1 Score: 89.66%
  • Test Recall: 87.59%
  • Test Loss: 0.0929

This translates to detecting approximately 87.6% of all potential wind turbine failures while maintaining high overall accuracy.

Key Insights¶

1. Data Quality & Characteristics¶

  • Highly imbalanced dataset: Only 5.55% failure cases vs 94.45% normal operations
  • Clean data: Minimal missing values (<0.1%) and no duplicates
  • Sensor patterns: Most features show normal distributions with some featuring slight skewness and outliers
  • Feature relationships: Complex nonlinear patterns between sensor readings and failure outcomes

2. Model Evolution & Performance¶

  • Baseline model: Started with 83.7% recall, improved systematically through architecture enhancements
  • Class weight balancing: Critical for handling imbalanced data, significantly improved recall from ~83% to ~87%
  • Architecture optimization: Progressive improvements from single-layer to deep networks with regularization
  • Best performing model: Deep network with dropout layers, early stopping, and adaptive learning rate

3. Business Cost Implications¶

  • Current model catches 87.6% of failures: Prevents majority of expensive generator replacements
  • False positive rate: ~1.14% leads to unnecessary inspections but much lower cost impact
  • False negative rate: ~12.4% still results in some undetected failures requiring full replacement

Actionable Recommendations¶

Immediate Deployment Strategy¶

  1. Deploy Model 6 as the primary predictive maintenance system
  2. Set up automated alerts when failure probability exceeds 50% threshold
  3. Implement weekly model retraining with new sensor data to maintain accuracy
  4. Create dashboards for real-time monitoring of turbine health scores

Operational Improvements¶

  1. Preventive Maintenance Schedule:

    • Prioritize turbines with failure probability >30% for immediate inspection
    • Schedule maintenance for turbines with probability 15-30% within next maintenance cycle

  2. Resource Allocation:

    • Pre-position repair teams near high-risk turbines during peak season
    • Stock critical components based on predicted failure patterns
    • Optimize maintenance crew schedules using model predictions

Cost Optimization¶

  • Use model confidence scores to determine intervention urgency
  • Cost-benefit analysis: Model prevents ~87.6% of $50K+ replacements
  • Expected ROI: Significant savings through early detection and repair
